title: Physical and Chemical Change
seo_title: Year 8 Science: Physical and Chemical Change Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Compare physical and chemical changes, identify indicators of energy change in chemical reactions, and use word equations to show that atoms are rearranged and mass is conserved (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on physical and chemical change: indicators of a reaction, exothermic and endothermic reactions, word equations, combustion, rusting and conservation of mass. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: A chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change does not.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ask: has a new substance been made?

  • Physical changes (melting, dissolving, cutting) do not make new substances and are often easy to reverse.
  • Indicators of a chemical change: gas, an unexpected colour change, light, a temperature change, or a solid (precipitate).
  • Word equation: reactants → products. Atoms are rearranged, so the total mass stays the same in a closed container.
Example

Wood burns in a campfire. Physical or chemical?

ash, smoke and gases form

Answer: chemical

Example

A reaction in an open beaker loses 3 g. Why?

a gas escaped

Answer: the mass went into the air

Common mistakes

  • Calling melting or dissolving a chemical change.
  • Thinking mass is destroyed when a gas escapes.
  • Thinking every colour change is a reaction (mixing paints is physical).

faq.q: How do I tell a physical change from a chemical change?
faq.a: Ask whether a new substance has formed. Look for gas, light, a temperature change, an unexpected colour change or a precipitate.

faq.q: Why does mass seem to change in some reactions?
faq.a: If a gas escapes or joins from the air, the mass in the open container changes. In a sealed container, the total mass stays the same.

faq.q: What is the difference between exothermic and endothermic?
faq.a: Exothermic reactions release energy, so the surroundings warm up. Endothermic reactions take in energy, so the surroundings cool down.

items.q: What kind of change is a copper roof turning green?
c: a physical change, because only the state changes
a physical change, because only the shape changes
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
items.e: A copper roof turning green makes a new substance with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

items.q: What kind of change is water vapour condensing on a mirror?
c: a physical change, because no new substance forms
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a chemical change, because it gives off light
items.e: Water vapour condensing on a mirror changes the shape, size, state or mixture, but the substances stay the same.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Bread dough rising with yeast makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: What is an endothermic reaction?
c: a reaction that gives out heat
a reaction that takes in energy, so the surroundings get colder
a reaction that makes light only
items.e: A sports cold pack gets cold because the reaction is endothermic.

items.q: Why does a steel boat trailer rust faster near the beach at the Gold Coast?
c: Salty, damp air speeds up the reaction of iron with oxygen and water.
items.e: Rusting is a chemical change that needs oxygen and water.

items.q: What kind of change is baking a cake?
c: a physical change, because only the state changes
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a physical change, because only the shape changes
items.e: Baking a cake makes a new substance with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

c: a physical change, because no new substance forms
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a chemical change, because it gives off light
items.e: Dissolving sugar in tea changes the shape, size, state or mixture, but the substances stay the same.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
c: food being digested in your stomach
items.e: Food being digested in your stomach makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

c: a chemical change, because a new substance forms

a physical change, because no new substance forms
items.e: Stretching a rubber band changes the shape, size, state or mixture, but the substances stay the same.

items.q: Mia observes that an apple slice turns brown in the air. Is this a chemical change or a physical change?
c: a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a physical change, because only the shape or state changes
a physical change, because it is a mixture
items.e: Gas, colour change, new smell, light, heat or a new solid are signs of a new substance.

c: a physical change, because only the shape changes
a chemical change, because a new substance forms
a physical change, because only the state changes
items.e: An iron bike chain rusting makes a new substance with new properties, so it is a chemical change.

items.q: Which is a physical change?

items.e: Tearing a sheet of foil does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

c: a chemical change, because a new substance forms

a physical change, because it is a mixture
items.e: Gas, colour change, new smell, light, heat or a new solid are signs of a new substance.

c: a physical change, because only the shape or state changes

items.e: Gas, colour change, new smell, light, heat or a new solid are signs of a new substance.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: A sliced apple turning brown makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Cooking a sausage on a barbecue: physical or chemical change?
c: chemical: new substances form and it cannot be uncooked
items.e: Cooking food is a chemical change.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: Breaking a glass does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Wax melts. What does this observation tell you?
c: It is a sign of a chemical reaction (a new substance may have formed).
It is a physical change, not a sign of a new substance.
items.e: Look for new substances.

items.q: In a bushfire, eucalyptus trees burn. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change: wood reacts with oxygen to make carbon dioxide, water and ash
a physical change: the wood dissolves
a physical change: the wood melts
items.e: Burning (combustion) is a chemical change.

items.q: A nail left outside turns red-brown and flaky. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
c: a new colour and a new solid
items.e: The observation shows a new colour and a new solid, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: What is a chemical reaction?
c: a process in which atoms rearrange to form new substances with new properties
a change of state like melting
items.e: New substances have different properties.

items.q: Noah lists changes around the house. Which is a physical change?
c: a glow stick is bent and starts to glow
an iron nail rusts in damp air
food is digested in the stomach
items.e: The substance stays the same.

items.q: A solid (precipitate) forms when two solutions are mixed. What does this observation tell you?
c: It is a sign of a chemical reaction (a new substance may have formed).
It is a physical change, not a sign of a new substance.
items.e: Look for new substances.

items.q: Harper lists changes around the house. Which is a physical change?
c: a glow stick is bent and starts to glow
bicarb soda and vinegar fizz and make a gas
food is digested in the stomach
items.e: The substance stays the same.

items.q: A glass breaks into pieces. What does this observation tell you?
c: It is a sign of a chemical reaction (a new substance may have formed).
It is a physical change, not a sign of a new substance.
items.e: Look for new substances.

items.q: A substance has a melting point of 0 °C and a boiling point of 100 °C. What is it most likely?
items.e: Those are water's characteristic properties.

items.q: Water boils and makes bubbles. Is this evidence of a chemical reaction?
c: Yes, all bubbles mean a reaction.
No. The bubbles are water vapour, the same substance.
items.e: Boiling is a change of state.

items.q: The temperature changes. What does this observation tell you?
c: It is a physical change, not a sign of a new substance.
It is a sign of a chemical reaction (a new substance may have formed).
items.e: Look for new substances.

c: bicarb soda and vinegar fizz and make a gas
items.e: A new substance with new properties forms.

items.q: Salt dissolves in water. What does this observation tell you?
c: It is a sign of a chemical reaction (a new substance may have formed).
It is a physical change, not a sign of a new substance.
items.e: Look for new substances.

items.q: Milk left out for days smells sour. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a new smell, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Matilda lists changes in the kitchen. Which is a chemical change?
c: chocolate is melted and poured into a mould
an iron nail rusts in damp air
items.e: A new substance with new properties forms.

items.e: The observation shows light and heat, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: An antacid tablet is dropped in water and fizzes. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows gas bubbles, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: What is the main difference between a physical change and a chemical change?
c: A physical change always involves heat.
A chemical change makes a new substance; a physical change does not.
A chemical change can always be reversed.
items.e: Melting ice is still water.

items.q: Burning a log produces ash, smoke and gases. What does this show?
c: New substances formed, so it is a chemical reaction.
items.e: The ash has different properties from wood.

items.q: Amelia lists changes in the kitchen. Which is a chemical change?
c: butter softens in a warm room
clay is shaped into a bowl
a glow stick is bent and starts to glow
items.e: A new substance with new properties forms.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? zinc + copper chloride → zinc chloride + copper
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Which are the reactants in this reaction? iron + sulfur → iron(II) sulfide
items.e: Reactants are on the left of the arrow.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? copper + oxygen → copper oxide
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: What is made when hydrogen burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: Which are the reactants in this reaction? calcium + oxygen → calcium oxide
items.e: Reactants are on the left of the arrow.

items.q: What is made when carbon (charcoal) burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: What is the product? copper + oxygen → ?
items.e: The elements combine to form a compound.

items.q: What is the product? hydrogen + oxygen → ?
items.e: The elements combine to form a compound.

items.q: Which is an indicator of a chemical change?
c: an unexpected colour change and a gas forming
items.e: Colour, gas, light, heat or a precipitate can show a new substance.

items.q: What is made when candle wax (a hydrocarbon) burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: What is the product? sodium + chlorine → ?
items.e: The elements combine to form a compound.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? copper carbonate → copper oxide + carbon dioxide
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: What is the product? iron + sulfur → ?
items.e: The elements combine to form a compound.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? magnesium + copper sulfate → magnesium sulfate + copper
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Which type of reaction is this? sulfuric acid + potassium hydroxide → potassium sulfate + water
items.e: Combustion: burning in oxygen. Thermal decomposition: heat breaks one compound into simpler ones. Neutralisation: acid + alkali → salt + water.

items.q: Which are the reactants in this reaction? hydrogen + oxygen → water
items.e: Reactants are on the left of the arrow.

items.q: Which are the reactants in this reaction? zinc + sulfur → zinc sulfide
items.e: Reactants are on the left of the arrow.

items.q: Write the word equation for burning methane (natural gas).
items.e: Reactants are on the left, products on the right.

items.q: What is made when propane burns completely in plenty of oxygen?
items.e: Hydrocarbons burn to carbon dioxide and water.

items.q: 36 g of magnesium burns in air and joins with 24 g of oxygen. What mass of magnesium oxide forms?
items.e: The magnesium gains the mass of the oxygen: 36 + 24.

items.q: Dissolving sugar in water: physical or chemical change?
c: physical: the sugar can be recovered by evaporating the water
items.e: Dissolving does not make a new substance.

items.q: Sugar turns into black carbon when heated strongly. What causes this chemical change?
items.e: Chemical changes can be caused by mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electricity.

items.q: 25 g of calcium carbonate is heated and breaks down. 11 g of carbon dioxide escapes. What mass of calcium oxide is left?
items.e: Mass of products = mass of reactant: 25 − 11 = 14 g.

items.q: 32 g of copper is heated in air and reacts completely with 8 g of oxygen. What mass of copper(II) oxide is formed?
items.e: Mass is conserved: 32 + 8 = 40 g.

items.q: 50 g of calcium carbonate is heated and breaks down. 22 g of carbon dioxide escapes. What mass of calcium oxide is left?
items.e: Mass of products = mass of reactant: 50 − 22 = 28 g.

items.q: Vinegar and bicarb soda fizz when mixed. What causes this chemical change?
items.e: Chemical changes can be caused by mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electricity.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 50 g of vinegar and a small cup with 20 g of bicarb soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 50 + 20 = 70 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 150 g of vinegar and a small cup with 25 g of bicarb soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 150 + 25 = 175 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: 100 g of calcium carbonate is heated and breaks down. 44 g of carbon dioxide escapes. What mass of calcium oxide is left?
items.e: Mass of products = mass of reactant: 100 − 44 = 56 g.

items.q: Marble chips react with acid in an open beaker on a balance. The mass shown goes down from 240 g to 238 g. Why?
c: Carbon dioxide gas escapes into the air.
Mass is destroyed in the reaction.
items.e: Mass is conserved; the gas leaves the beaker.

items.q: A 60 g solution is mixed with a 20 g solution in a sealed flask and a solid forms. What is the total mass now?
items.e: No atoms escape a sealed flask, so the mass stays the same.

items.q: Isla mixes 25 g of one solution with 15 g of another in a sealed flask. A precipitate forms. What is the total mass after the reaction?
items.e: Mass is conserved: no atoms are created or destroyed.

items.q: Water splits into hydrogen and oxygen in an electrolysis cell. What causes this chemical change?
items.e: Chemical changes can be caused by mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electricity.

items.q: What are the reactants in: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide?
items.e: Reactants are the starting substances.

items.q: Amelia puts 25 g of marble chips and acid in an open flask. After the reaction it has a mass of 21 g. Why is it lighter?
c: Carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air.
Mass is not conserved in reactions.
items.e: The gas leaves the open flask: 4 g of it.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 80 g of vinegar and a small cup with 10 g of bicarb soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 80 + 10 = 90 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: 24 g of magnesium burns in air and joins with 16 g of oxygen. What mass of magnesium oxide forms?
items.e: The magnesium gains the mass of the oxygen: 24 + 16.

items.q: A sealed bag holds 150 g of vinegar and a small cup with 10 g of bicarb soda. The bag is tipped so they mix and the bag puffs up. What is the total mass now?
items.e: A new gas forms, but the bag is sealed, so nothing gets out: 150 + 10 = 160 g. The particles are rearranged, not destroyed.

items.q: Photographic film darkens. What causes this chemical change?
items.e: Chemical changes can be caused by mixing, heating, light, oxygen or electricity.

items.q: Zara burns 1 g of magnesium ribbon and collects all the ash. It has a mass of about 1.7 g. Why is it heavier?
c: Oxygen from the air joined with the magnesium.
items.e: Magnesium oxide includes the oxygen atoms.

items.q: Is crushing a can a physical change or a chemical change?
c: a chemical change, because it looks different
a chemical change, because a new substance is formed
a physical change, because no new substance is formed
items.e: Look for a new substance: a colour change, gas, heat or light that cannot easily be reversed.

items.q: What is the test for carbon dioxide?
items.e: Thermal decomposition of carbonates.

items.q: Kai puts iron nails in tap water, salt water and dry air for a week. Which nail rusts most?
items.e: Salt speeds up rusting; dry air slows it.

items.q: Copper(II) carbonate is green. When heated, it turns black and gives off a gas that turns limewater milky. What has happened?
c: thermal decomposition, forming copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide
items.e: Limewater detects carbon dioxide.

items.q: Tom puts a steel wool pad in a jar with a little water and seals it. After a week it is orange. Why does he also keep a dry steel wool pad in a sealed jar?
c: to see if water is needed for rusting
items.e: Comparing wet and dry steel wool shows whether water affects rusting.

items.q: Which change is both a chemical change and useful to us?
items.e: Cooking makes food easier to digest.

items.q: Magnesium ribbon burns with a bright white light and forms a white powder. Why is the powder heavier than the ribbon?
c: Oxygen from the air has combined with the magnesium.
items.e: Mass of product = mass of magnesium + oxygen.

items.q: Mia mixes vinegar and bicarb soda in an open beaker. The mass drops from 150 g to 146 g. Why?
c: Carbon dioxide gas escaped into the air.
items.e: In a closed container, the mass would stay the same.

items.q: A student says that burning paper is a physical change because the paper only changes shape. Why is he wrong?
c: Paper is not made of atoms.
The mass stays the same in an open room.
Burning is a change of state.
New substances (ash, carbon dioxide and water) are formed.
items.e: Burning cannot be reversed.

items.q: Which question can be answered by mixing two substances and observing?
c: Does mixing vinegar and bicarb soda make a new substance?
items.e: You can test it in class: mix them, observe the bubbles and compare properties.

items.q: Is digesting food in the stomach a physical change or a chemical change?
c: a chemical change, because the change can always be reversed
a physical change, because no new substance is formed
a chemical change, because a new substance is formed
items.e: Look for a new substance: a colour change, gas, heat or light that cannot easily be reversed.

items.q: Two cups of milk are left out, one in a warm room and one in the fridge. Which will most likely smell sour first?
c: the milk in the warm room
items.e: Souring is a chemical change made by tiny living things. It happens faster when it is warm.

items.q: Is striking a match a physical change or a chemical change?
c: a chemical change, because a new substance is formed
a chemical change, because the change can always be reversed
a physical change, because no new substance is formed
items.e: Look for a new substance: a colour change, gas, heat or light that cannot easily be reversed.

items.q: Which safety rule is most important when testing mixtures in class?
c: Wear safety goggles and never taste the mixtures.
Mix as many things as possible.
items.e: Unknown mixtures can be harmful. Goggles protect your eyes, and you should never taste them.

items.q: What is the test for oxygen?
items.e: Supports burning.

items.q: Mia drops the same size antacid tablet into cold water and hot water. Which variable is she testing?
items.e: Only the water temperature is different, so that is the variable she is testing.

items.q: What is an exothermic reaction?
c: one that transfers energy to the surroundings, so they get warmer
one that takes in energy and gets colder
items.e: Burning, respiration.

items.q: Ella wants a fair test of how temperature affects how fast a tablet fizzes. What should she keep the same?
c: the volume of water and the size of the tablet
items.e: Only the temperature should change.

items.q: Ruby measures the temperature of a reaction: 21 °C at the start, 29 °C after 2 minutes. What does this show?
items.e: The temperature rose, so energy was released.
